Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

Vignette:
Tariq was nineteen when he finally sat in the intake office, the memory of his childhood still anchored in the physical world rather than floating as abstract fear. His caregiver’s hands, heavy and unpredictable, had turned the family kitchen into a space where safety depended entirely on posture and silence. A raised voice could precede a shove; a sudden reach for his shoulder felt less like affection and more like control. He had learned to read the room long before he could read a weather report, watching the tension in his caregiver’s jaw, the way a clenched fist preceded a strike. Those early years did not fade when he grew older. Instead, they hardened into a quiet habit of scanning, leaving him sensitive to the exact shape of sound and movement around him. In the bright, open-plan laboratory where he worked as an environmental scientist, Tariq kept his back pressed to the glass partition. He never sat in the center of the long wooden tables. He always chose the edge seat with a solid wall at his right side, a position that let him watch the room without being boxed in. His eyes moved constantly over the faces of his colleagues, cataloguing microexpressions and shifts in posture. When a colleague leaned too close, Tariq felt a familiar tightening in his chest. He did not know why the contact felt so sharp, only that his body had decided, long ago, that unexpected touch meant something was about to change. Over the years, his avoidance patterns had woven themselves into his daily rhythm. He steered clear of situations that might spark disagreement, often nodding through project reviews rather than speaking up. He avoided being alone in a room, preferring to stay in hallways or linger near the sample preparation area where the low hum of centrifuges kept the quiet at bay. He avoided other people altogether on weekends, finding the crowded grocery store and the bustling café unnecessarily loud. His wife, Laila, had watched these patterns settle over him. She remembered the months when he stopped answering her calls, not because he did not care, but because the phone ringing felt like a summons he had not prepared for. Their marriage had not fractured, but it had shifted into a quieter orbit. He would cook meals beside her, yet often eat at the counter, keeping the distance between them as if it were a natural buffer. When his specific triggers surfaced, they arrived with a clarity that made his routines feel necessary. A sudden argument on television made him look away, his jaw working silently. When Laila cried, he would set down his book and watch her carefully, his attention fixed on the shape of her tears rather than the words she spoke. The unpredictability of crying unsettled him; it was an affective display that felt both vulnerable and volatile. Once, when a junior researcher patted his shoulder without warning, Tariq had flinched so sharply he had knocked over a beaker. He had not apologized immediately. He had simply straightened his lab coat and retreated to his wall-anchored desk, where he spent the rest of the afternoon examining soil samples with methodical precision. By the time he sat in the therapist’s office, Tariq’s life had become a careful arrangement of boundaries. He had come to believe that watching faces was the only way to navigate a room that still felt occasionally unsteady. His field assignments had grown rare. The open plots removed his wall and his safe seat, leaving him exposed to the weather and the unpredictable contact of fellow researchers. He did not know if he should change these habits or simply live alongside them. What he knew was that he was tired of constantly measuring the distance between himself and the room, and he had come to seek help because he wanted to understand why a simple touch or a raised voice could still feel like a storm rolling in.
